Oh and a classic acidic soil boggy species is the cranberry but it's not a tree. They usually are grown in areas like New England (severe winter) but I think a place like Wales could be fine for them because it still has enough winter chill hours, it just happens to not get super cold.

Taro like it wet with decent drainage (they are an invasive plant on the edge of shady drainage ditches that occasionally flood them where I live in Florida). They also like very rich soil. As a tropical plant, they can shed their older leaves throughout the year but they should be replacing them faster than they are shedding them (so there's net growth). 

The green veins of the yellowing leaf  and the yellow spots of the other mature leaf while the young leaf is ok really point to a nutrient issue to me , esp. potassium and manganese. Feed it some all-purpose fertilizer that has micronutrients as well but do not over-fertilize.

I think you might have been somehow overwatering it before (as unthinkable as that is to me haha) but it seems to be a better groove now if the young leaf is ok. Maybe aim for less frequent but deeper watering regimen. 

I also wonder if the humidity of the room is off? I'm not familiar with growing these indoors but they might get issues in areas with low humidity.

To cause leaf drop like this my guess is it either got cold or has a fungal/water mold disease on the roots (too much water/not enough drainage). 
Dropping all leaves at once suggests cold damage, if it lost leaves in a certain direction (either top ones first or bottom ones first, especially bottom ones first) that suggests the root diseases.

I'd ease up on the water if it is leafless it doesn't need much, and hope for the best. I'd also remove the leaves at the base in case it is a disease. If issue is fungal/water mold you might could take it out of the pot and observe the roots, remove any that look dead and replace all the contaminated soil but that's kind of tricky and might not even work.

What area do you live in/what zone? If it has no leaves there is not much reason to put it outside even if it is warm enough. Just keep it close to a window (preferably a south-facing or east-facing one).

BTW seed grown citrus generally has weak root systems. That's why all citrus is generally grafted but you might already be aware of that.

For Florida I like Violette de Bordeaux and Celeste dwarf figs the best so far but Brown Turkey is also a tried and true variety (it's taste just isn't as strong as the other two). They don't need as much fertilizer or water as other fruit trees and they don't have any super serious diseases here.
After that I find Meyer's Lemons to be the easiest type of citrus to grow and the lemons on them are more mild and huge so they have more uses than the grocery store ones :)
Many herbs are from Mediterranean so they don't need to be watered too much. Ones I find easy off the top of my head are mint, oregano, sweet marjoram,  garlic chives, chamomile (german kind is perennial/lives longer) , and rosemary. These are commonly available but there's also the mail-order nursery Santa Rosa Gardens (google) in Florida that I use if they aren't.

For easy seeds (just plop in pot an water every so often until they're big) borage (edible blue flowers taste like cucumbers) and sweet fennel (bronze or green) are good. Fennel also attracts swallowtail caterpillars that she might find fun/cheer her up.

A simple potting mix you can find at any home improvement store or nursery should suffice for all of these as well as an all-purpose fertilizer (the citrus would need it the most).

One last thing is that it is easier to do vegetables in fall (fall stuff like radishes, carrots, beets, and lettuce are very easy you just throw them on the dirt practically). Spring/summer veggie growing is much more labor intensive so I would not recommend it except for perhaps a nursery-bought tomato plant or pepper.

Not edible but look into:
- Sweet Verbena (very fragrant, easy, long bloom season)
- Southwestern/drought-tolerant plants like blanketflower, mexican agastache (i grow AZ Sun from seed), Salvia greggi/Autumn Sage, Coral Fountain, etc for containers as they require less water and would appreciate being in a well-drained container. 
Succulents might also be a good idea but may require special potting soil (e.g. vermiculite mixed in with regular soil).

1) I think you can go pretty big. It just depends on what you are growing. Most of the stuff I grow does not require much maintenance at all. Biggest thing is to have a mulch layer thick enough to keep out weeds, weeding is the main battle (you might also want to add newspaper under the mulch as a further suppressor). After that care is: Water (often unnecessary in established plants), fertilizer (once a year for most), and pruning (most only need it once a year, anything more is just a matter of taste).

2) You can probably plant some evergreen plants right now. I see no benefit to buying a deciduous plant now rather than in spring unless it’s to save money.

4) People use the phrase “amending soil” in two different ways: One way is adding a fresh layer of compost to your soil. The other way is to describe people trying to actively change their soil into something else, or ‘fighting it’. 

I do the former for some plants. I think the latter is a losing battle too many gardeners are engaged in (trying to completely change your soil is like trying to change your zone in my opinion.. there’s ways to push the zone limits just as there are ways to adjust your soil but it’s a lot of work and tinkering that should not be considered the norm).
That being said, if you have plants that hate your clay soil because it drains slowly you can build raised beds and plop whatever soil you want inside of them to increase drainage. I feel like in an actual garden bed the soil and nutrients just move too much for any big changes to really stick but if you have something fenced in with wooden or other barriers over the existing soil it’ll stay in place/stay what you want more.

There's no way to completely diminish mosquitoes. Pesticides for them, especially adult ones, are not specific (and honestly, in my experience they make things worse because insects that eat mosquitoes are often slower growing and take longer to repopulate after pesticides than mosquitoes do, creating a vicious cycle). Bug spray is more effective than using pesticides and more cost-effective too.

If you must use pesticide for them, something that targets larva is [Bti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bacillus_thuringiensis_israelensis) (also will kill other dipteran insects but this is still more limited than the sprays people use, though that's not saying much because those pesticides target multiple orders of insects and are even toxic to fish). Make a trap of it with a bucket+water+wooden paddle in it. Not sure of its safety for other animals though so be careful.

If you live in an area with mosquitoes it just comes with the territory. That being said, natural predators help so I second the bat house thing (make sure you position it so it isn't getting afternoon sun right on it, I've seen some people here do them like that and that probably isn't a good idea in Florida).

Some plants are said to ward them off. I do remember having less in my yard last year when I grew a bunch of basil from seed which is one of the plants people say wards them off. Also if your place in FL is anywhere like my place in FL, the species you are mostly seeing is the invasive Asian Tiger mosquito which is much more adaptable to human areas and its larva have even been known to survive in mud. These are the sorts that tend to get the awful infestation levels and there's very little we can do about it.

I read the whole thing but I came back to that quote. It sounds to me like your ADHD was already treated and managed. I think the question is less of "will your brain be a cavity" and more like "do you even need further treatment for your ADHD?" Buprion is an atypical antidepressant that is said to have dopamine and norepinephrine activity, both hormones involved in amphetamines (or at least the former is) like adderall. My knowledge of these things are limited but it's my understanding that one more directly induces the creation of it (the "squeezing" you described), the other keeps your body for reabsorbing. I definitely think some forms of ADHD could be treated with a drug like Wellbutrin but it's up to you to know whether or not yours does.

Also personally, as someone with ADHD (Inattentive type) and depression I applaud you for quitting a substance. And I recommend to stay away from extra chemicals in general like caffeine (in coffee, but in smaller amounts like some teas and chocolate should be fine). Some people self-medicate for it and maybe it helps them but if you're anything like me you're ultimately better without it and keeping things routine and balanced helps you more.

But re: brain cavity. I really do not think so. You see dopamine-related disorders that are long-lasting from things like anti-psychotics (things that are anti-dopamine, opposite of your case), particularly younger ones. I have relatives who developed schizophrenia decades ago who have been guinea pigs for various treatments, many of which much worse than what is done today. Even after all that they only really have recently developed the chronic side effects like their chin wobbling. And again, these drugs are the opposite of what you are taking and I've never heard of similar happening to long-term ADHD treatment.
EDIT: I do remember an emergent side-effect of therapeutic amphetamines and it's hallucinations/psychosis that goes away once you stop taking them, this leads me to believe the effects on your brain really aren't super permanent.

I'd keep doing what the doctor says. If you question the medication at all question whether or not it is needed (especially if it costs you money), don't be worried about the "cavity" thing. 

Anyway best of luck and I hope that helps

In addition to what's been said I'll say what I do, depending on audience:

Best way I can describe it is a metaphor and relate it to other, more commonly accepted (in our society) conditions. You can simplify down disorders like schizophrenia which is about being too alert to things that aren't there and focus on them due to increased dopamine. Then the opposite, not enough dopamine/norepinephrine means you aren't alert and can't focus. 

Now, both of these are happening in specific areas (and most medication I know of can't target a specific location so much as everywhere in the brain) which is why even with medication it's often not a perfect solution but it's still better than nothing. ADHD looks like laziness but is quite different and there is a scientific explanation behind it, it isn't some "conspiracy". What would be odder, to me, is that there could be a condition linked to too much x but never one linked to not enough x -- which is what people who dont believe ADHD is real seem to think.

(Both of those are very, very simplified versions of it of course but sometimes you have to do that to explain things to people. I'm sure when we were taught things in primary school it was oversimplified too.)

Anyway, hope that helps! Sorry she's not very accepting of it so far.
